instructions: Pat the steak dry and cut it into 4 even pieces. In a bowl, mix the oyster sauce, the soy sauce, the sugar, the garlic (mince it first), 1/2 tsp of the pepper and 1 tbsp of the oil. Add the steak and turn to coat. Leave it on the counter for 30 minutes.
Meanwhile, slice the onion into thin wedges. Slice the cucumber into rounds and halve the cherry tomatoes if they're large. Cut the baguette into 4 pieces.
Make the dip. In a small bowl, mix 1 tsp of the salt and 1 tsp of the pepper, then squeeze in the juice of half the lime and stir. Cut the other half into wedges.

Heat a large cast iron or heavy skillet over medium-high heat for 2 minutes. Add 1 tbsp of the oil and the onion. Cook for 5 minutes, stirring now and then, until soft and browned at the edges. Transfer to a plate.

Add the last 1 tbsp oil to the skillet and raise the heat to high. Lay in the steak and leave it alone for 3 minutes, until the underside is deep brown and lets go of the pan. Stand back a little. It will spatter.

Flip the steak. Add 2 tbsp of the butter and spoon it over the steak as it melts. Cook for 3 minutes. You're cooking it to 130°F in the middle for medium-rare, so if you have a thermometer, check it there. No thermometer? Cut into the thickest piece: it should be pink in the middle.
Transfer the steak to a cutting board and let it rest for 5 minutes. Slice it across the grain into strips about 1/2 inch thick.
Return the skillet to medium-high heat. Add the tomatoes and the remaining 1/2 tsp salt and cook for 2 minutes, until blistered. Transfer to the plate with the onion.
Lower the heat to medium. Melt the remaining 2 tbsp butter in the skillet. Crack in the eggs and cook for 2 to 3 minutes, until the whites are set and the yolks are still runny.
Taste a slice of the steak. If it's flat, add a pinch more salt.
Divide the steak, onion, tomatoes and eggs among 4 plates. Add a spoonful of the liver pâté, the cucumber and the lime wedge to each. Serve with the baguette and the lime-pepper dip.
method_notes: The sources agree on a quickly seared, oyster-sauce-marinated steak with a fried egg, tomato, onion, pâté, a lime, salt and pepper dip, and bread. They differ on size and style: Cooking Therapy sears one thick steak, Vicky Pham slices the beef thin and cooks it in small batches, and Vietnam Discovery adds fries and pounds the beef. I followed the lead's method but cut the steak into four pieces and sliced it after resting so it serves four. No version has 20 or more ratings (the lead shows 5 from 6 on the page, JSON-LD not shown), so this is a fallback lead; this dish is also called bò né.
